title: Almost-linear-time \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximation of edit distance
formal:
For every fixed rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), does there exist one uniform classical randomized algorithm \(A_\varepsilon\) which, on every pair of explicitly given strings \(x,y\) of total length \(n=|x|+|y|\geq2\), outputs an integer \(D\) such that
\[\Pr\bigl[\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\leq D\leq(1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\bigr]\geq\frac23,\]
and has worst-case running time \(n^{1+o(1)}\) in the word-RAM model below? Here \(\operatorname{ED}\) is unit-cost Levenshtein distance, the probability is only over the algorithm’s independent random bits, and the time bound must hold on every execution. For each fixed accuracy, the same algorithm must satisfy every positive fixed exponent slack.
definitions:
For total length \(n\), let \(\Sigma_n=\{0,1,\ldots,n^2+1\}\). The input consists of two lengths \(p,q\geq0\) with \(p+q=n\geq2\), and arrays \(x\in\Sigma_n^p\), \(y\in\Sigma_n^q\), one symbol per word. Either string may be empty. The lengths and all \(n\) symbols are given explicitly in consecutive input cells, not by a compressed representation or an oracle.

The distance \(\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\) is the minimum length of a finite sequence of edits transforming \(x\) into \(y\). An edit inserts one alphabet symbol at any position, deletes one symbol, or replaces one symbol by another. Each edit costs one; leaving a matching symbol unchanged costs zero. All intermediate strings use \(\Sigma_n\). Insertions and deletions can shift later positions. There are no block moves, transpositions, symbol-dependent weights or affine gap costs. In particular, this is not the distance that forbids substitutions and charges two for a replacement. The minimum is a nonnegative integer and at most \(n\).

For each fixed \(\varepsilon\), the machine may choose an integer \(B_\varepsilon\geq3\); its word length on total length \(n\) is
\[w=B_\varepsilon\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil.\]
A word is an unsigned integer from \(0\) to \(2^w-1\). Memory addresses are words, input cells contain the explicit lengths and arrays, and the remaining memory is initially zero. The program is one finite instruction sequence independent of \(n\), with a fixed finite list of integer constants. Unit-cost instructions are a word read or write at a word address, a comparison, conditional branch, a bitwise Boolean operation, a logical shift, addition, subtraction or multiplication modulo \(2^w\), or integer quotient or remainder with a nonzero word divisor. A logical shift fills with zeros, discards overflow, and returns zero when its shift amount is at least \(w\). Address calculations are charged under the same rules. Larger integers occupy multiple words and require multiple charged instructions. There is no arbitrary-precision arithmetic or precomputed input-dependent table at unit cost. Each draw of one independent fair random bit costs one instruction. Runtime includes all preprocessing, random draws and output writing. No advice, oracle, preprocessed database or quantum operations are provided.

The output is an integer in signed binary notation, with every written word charged. Only its numerical value is required; an edit script is not. On a failed random execution it may be outside the specified interval. Success must have probability at least \(2/3\) separately for every fixed input pair, regardless of its distance. Thus equal strings require output zero on successful executions, and no additive error depending on \(n\) is permitted.

Let \(T_{A_\varepsilon}(n)\) be the maximum number of instructions over all valid pairs of total length \(n\) and all random-bit sequences. It must be finite for every \(n\geq2\). The asymptotic requirement is
\[\forall\eta\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\;\exists C_{\varepsilon,\eta}>0\;\exists N_{\varepsilon,\eta}\geq2\;\forall n\geq N_{\varepsilon,\eta}:\quad
T_{A_\varepsilon}(n)\leq C_{\varepsilon,\eta}n^{1+\eta}.\]
Here the threshold is an integer. The choice of program and \(B_\varepsilon\) comes before \(\eta\). They may depend on the fixed accuracy but not on an exponent slack later used to describe their runtime. The accuracy is not an additional varying input. There is no requirement that the algorithms for different accuracies be generated effectively from \(\varepsilon\), no polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\), and no common constants across accuracies. This preserves the saved fixed-accuracy interpretation. The notation \(n^{1+o(1)}\) specifies the displayed upper bounds; it is not an expected-time guarantee or a requirement of a fixed polylogarithmic overhead.
answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated existence for every fixed rational accuracy, or of its logical negation. A positive answer must establish the per-input success guarantee and every-execution runtime for one algorithm per accuracy, with the complete quantifier order above. A negative answer must establish some fixed rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) for which no permitted algorithm and word-size constant meet both guarantees. It must rule out randomized algorithms, not only deterministic ones. A conditional lower bound proves only a conditional conclusion unless its assumption is also proved. A different algorithm for each exponent slack, a constant factor not arbitrarily close to one, an additive-error estimate, an expected-time bound alone, or a result restricted to special strings does not settle this target. This is an algorithm-existence question with the stated relative-error parameter, not a numerical target with a separate additive tolerance.
why: Edit distance captures sequence alignment under insertions and deletions as well as replacements. The question asks whether every pair of long sequences can be compared with arbitrarily small fixed relative error while the worst-case time exponent approaches the input-reading exponent one. It would resolve a central joint accuracy–runtime frontier beyond both constant-factor approximation and a fixed saving over quadratic time.

importance.reason: A central accuracy–runtime frontier for sequence comparison, with recent work on each side of the tradeoff. It is a genuinely stronger near-exact runtime target than TCS-7220, retained under the user’s explicit acceptance of related edit-distance questions.

context_blocks.text: Rubinstein’s July 2018 research exposition explicitly asks in Open question 2 for arbitrarily accurate multiplicative approximation in truly subquadratic or near-linear time. The present card records the user-approved almost-linear branch with a precise single-algorithm meaning. The post’s later update strikes out a different question, about a constant factor; it does not mark the near-exact question solved.

Andoni and Nosatzki obtain, for each fixed runtime slack \(\eta>0\), a randomized \(O(n^{1+\eta})\)-time approximation with factor \(f(1/\eta)\). Theorem 1.1 of the checked full manuscript makes the factor depend on the slack; the following paragraph describes that dependence as doubly exponential. The August 2026 journal publication retains the fixed-slack result. Neither arbitrarily small fixed relative error nor a single fixed approximation constant surviving \(\eta\to0\) follows from it.

Mao and Rubinstein’s 2026 approximation scheme provides a \((1+\varepsilon)\)-estimate for each fixed positive \(\varepsilon\), with stated time \(n^2/2^{\log^{\Omega(1)}n}\). Their Theorem 6.1 gives success probability at least \(1-1/n\). This is a substantial speedup over quadratic time, but its stated bound does not establish the almost-linear target here. The theorem concerns ordinary edit distance with substitutions; its separate multiplicative approximation for longest common subsequence has a different objective.

Backurs and Indyk relate a fixed exponent saving for exact edit distance to a fixed exponential saving for CNF satisfiability. This supports a conditional barrier for exact computation. It is not a hardness theorem for every fixed multiplicative accuracy, and does not refute the present randomized approximation question. In particular, replacing a fixed accuracy by an input-length-dependent tolerance that forces exactness changes the quantifiers.

Three retained cards describe different frontiers. TCS-7220 asks for \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximation with a positive fixed saving from exponent two for each accuracy. This card asks for the stronger exponent-one limit. TCS-6624 instead allows any one fixed constant approximation factor but requires time \(O(n(\log(n+2))^d)\) for one fixed \(d\). An \(n^{1+o(1)}\) upper bound alone need not have such a polylogarithmic overhead. The near-exact target here implies the weaker time target of TCS-7220, but it is not identified with the different accuracy–time combination of TCS-6624.

The small-distance regime is part of the question. When the true distance is zero, successful output must be zero, and a growing additive error cannot be hidden by the multiplicative factor. Guarantees for distant pairs, random inputs, indexed codewords, compressed strings, or tree edit distance have different hypotheses or objects. The question asks only for the value estimate on arbitrary explicitly stored strings.
